title: In a Cashless Society, There Is No Change
author: Mutually Assured Instruction
summary: This article diagnoses why school change initiatives so consistently fail, arguing that the root cause is misdiagnosis: schools implement solutions to problems they haven't accurately identified. Drawing on observations from Australian schools adopting explicit instruction, the author illustrates how a school can correctly identify the right intervention (explicit teaching, checking for understanding) but apply it to the wrong presenting problem — introducing CFU strategies into classrooms where attention and behavior regulation haven't been established first, creating conditions where teachers are checking for a lack of understanding because students weren't listening. The author calls this pattern 'shiny thing syndrome': the tendency, accelerated by technology cycles since the 1990s, to adopt new initiatives because of novelty rather than diagnosed need. Even well-supported pedagogical frameworks backed by government can fail when applied without root-cause analysis. The prescription is narrow focus, granular implementation, and sustained follow-up: rather than a single professional learning session covering all of classroom management, schools should spend an entire term focused only on entry routines, observing implementation, celebrating early adopters, and making iterative adjustments. Citing tipping-point research suggesting that 18–25% adoption is required before change becomes embedded, the author argues that without continued focus, a school is unlikely to ever reach more than 5% adoption of any initiative. The article ends with a sobering note: even the best-intentioned change is likely to fail if teachers are constantly being asked to absorb new shiny things — they become overworked, overburdened, and over it.
points: The central diagnostic failure in school change is applying a correct solution to an incorrectly identified problem — no level of explicit teaching can explicitly teach your way out of a school-wide behaviour regulation problem, so schools that implement CFU into chaotic classrooms are simply checking for a lack of understanding produced by inattention.

The 'shiny thing' cycle is structural: schools have been conditioned by tech-accelerated innovation cycles to expect revolutionary interventions and replace them quickly, making it nearly impossible to build the extended runway (18–25% tipping point adoption) that real culture change requires.

Focus on one thing — in such detail that it is more difficult for staff not to do it — is the author's core prescription: a single term on entry routines, with observation, public celebration of early adopters, and iterative adjustments, embeds more real change than a scattershot info-dump on all of classroom management.

The Shaquille O'Neal free-throw analogy frames the resource-allocation question precisely: a player whose weakness is the free throw line doesn't train equally on all aspects of his game — he goes to the line, repeatedly, under game conditions, until the specific weakness is addressed.

School leaders are themselves biased diagnosticians and may miss school needs in favour of their own portfolio strengths, which is why data triangulation (learning walks, staff surveys, student surveys, leadership opinions) is essential before choosing any intervention.
quotes: Would it shock you if I was to suggest that most change fails not because the idea was bad (although some are), but because the school hasn't taken the time to work out the true root cause of their current state? No level of explicit teaching can explicitly teach your way out of a school wide lapse in positive behaviours.

A school may be better served focussing on entry routines, classroom layouts and attention signals before even thinking about the next steps as we know from the Simple Model of the Mind that without attention there's no retention in working memory let alone long term memory. So by focussing on checking for understanding in classrooms where attention and behaviour is scattered at best, you're likely to simply be setting teachers up to be at the front of the room checking for a lack of understanding.

Whether it be a school leader resume padding, a charlatan consultant grifting your school with all show and no substance or even at times pedagogical frameworks supported by the government. The new shiny thing loses its luster pretty quickly when it gets put into practice. Fading faster than the haircut of a trendy teenager these initiatives do not realistically work in real classrooms.

The knowledge was imparted on staff and therefore they are now experts and all of the problems will be solved. Again, this is rarely presented this way maliciously, it is more often to 'respect' the experience of staff within the school. But if diving deep into educational research has taught me anything, the average school teacher knows a lot less about learning and classroom management than you'd ever expect.

Focus on one thing. Focus on that thing in such detail that it is more difficult for staff to not do it. Instead of a single one off professional learning session on all of Classroom Management, why not focus solely on Entry Routines and then continue to focus on it for at least 5 weeks if not a term.

Multiple studies suggest around a 18-25% tipping point before a change takes hold and becomes embedded within a school. Without continued focus on an initiative a school is unlikely to ever get more than 5%. Even the best intentioned change is likely to fail.

Staff actually want to do the best for their students, however when they're constantly having to adapt and add in shiny thing after shiny thing teaching starts to lose its lustre. They become overworked, overburdened and over it. We need to work out exactly what schools and staff need and attack the root cause of any issues first.
